title: A Snapshot of Influence: A Local Data Attribution Framework for Online Rei

predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: f^{return}(θ) is defined as E[ log π_θ(a|s) · (−Â^{ref}(s,a)) ]. The text claims that maximizing this function encourages increasing the probability of better-than-average actions and decreasing worse-than-average ones. However, because of the negative sign, maximizing f^{return} would increase log-probability for actions with negative advantage (worse-than-average) and decrease it for actions with positive advantage (better-than-average), which is the opposite of improving return. This sign error contradicts the stated interpretation and standard policy gradient direction.

predicted_errors.error_location: Section 5.3 versus Section 3.1 target function definitions
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: In Section 3.1, f^{return} is defined with a negative advantage term (−Â^{ref}), while in Section 5.3 the RLHF target function f^{seq} uses a plain Â^{ref}_{−1} without a negative sign. These two target functions are inconsistent in their handling of the advantage sign, yet both are intended to measure beneficial influence toward higher cumulative return/reward.

The paper states 'Kumar et al. [2024] demonstrated that data attribution methods can be directly applied to online RL without modification...' but no entry for Kumar et al. 2024 appears in the reference list. The citation is missing, making the claim unsupported and unverifiable.

The abstract claims 'IIF completely eliminates sample inefficiency, achieves unprecedented training speed, and solves the long-standing challenge of training instability in online RL.' The experiments show improvements in sample efficiency (20–67% reduction in training rounds) but do not demonstrate complete elimination of sample inefficiency; sample complexity still grows with task difficulty. Similarly, the claim of solving training instability is not adequately supported by the reported evidence.

The text first states 'we set the reference policy π^{ref} to a fixed, pre-trained policy that has been trained to convergence on the task.' Later it says 'Unlike a fixed, off-distribution reference that may provide misleading signals..., our dynamic reference evolves with training.' These statements contradict each other: a fixed pre-trained policy cannot be simultaneously evolving with training.

predicted_errors.error_location: Section 3.1, validation dataset selection for f^{return}
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The target function f^{return} is defined as an expectation over π^{ref} (a fixed pre-trained policy), but the paper states that the training rollout buffer B^{(k)} (collected under the current policy π_{θ^{(k)}}) can be directly used as the validation dataset. Using data from a different distribution (π_{θ^{(k)}} instead of π^{ref}) without importance weighting would give a biased estimate of the expectation and the resulting gradients, compromising the validity of the influence scores.
